newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget in surplus in 1998? Maybe. [CORRECTED 20:22 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget in surplus in 1998? Maybe. [CORRECTED 20:22 GMT]

text.p: A vibrant economy has created a tide of tax revenues that could wipe out the government's budget deficit as early as next year, some analysts say, though it might prove a brief respite.

"It is possible, even without a budget agreement (between Congress and the Clinton administration), that the budget could be in surplus in 1998," Allen Sinai, chief global economist with Primark Decision Economics Inc. in Boston, said Tuesday.

"The focus of the nation should now be on managing a surplus, not simply on deficit reduction," Sinai said, taking the opportunity to boost investment and build a cushion for the costs of caring for an ageing population of "baby boomers" after about 2010 when deficits are expected to mount again.
The United States has not posted a budget surplus since 1969, reaching a peak of red ink in fiscal 1992 when spending outstripped income by a staggering $290.4 billion.

With the economy now in its seventh year of unbroken expansion since the 1990-91 recession, dynamic job growth has meant a flood of individual tax payments into state, local and federal government coffers.
That is complemented by a brisk flow of corporate tax revenues from profitable businesses and a jump in capital gains taxes from a bull market on Wall Street that has sent stock prices soaring.
The unexpectedly bright budget picture has analysts scurrying to scale back forecasts for the shortfall between government income and spending in the current 1997 tax year that ends on Sept. 30.

While the Clinton administration remains officially on record as forecasting a $125.9 billion deficit, Wall Street analysts (corrects attribution) put it nearer $50 billion. The White House is expected to issue a revised lower estimate later this summer.
"The economy has simply grown at a much stronger rate than anyone expected," Sinai said. When that happens, there invariably is a surge in tax receipts that is never accounted for in forecasts.

"There's always an exaggerated response in tax behaviour at the extremes of the business cycle," Sinai said, adding the same phenomenon occurs in reverse when the economy heads into recession and revenues abruptly tail off.

Senators and members of the House of Representatives are set to bargain on separately passed versions of tax and spending proposals Thursday and Friday, with the White House interjecting when possible to arrive at a three-cornered pact for balancing the budget by 2002.

Economist Lynn Reaser of Barnett Banks Inc. in Jacksonville, Fla., worried that a buoyant economy may make it harder to come to grips with issues that should be dealt with, such as reining in costly entitlement programmes, including Social Security and Medicare.
"There may be less pressure to deal with current spending issues, less pressure to face up to future spending issues, more willingness to do more tax cuts," she said.

Reaser said it might be difficult to move into surplus in the near future, but pointed out that a deficit of $50 billion in the world's largest economy "is relatively close to balance" -- less than 1 percent of the $7 trillion worth of goods and services that make up U.S. gross domestic product.

By contrast, European countries, including Germany and France, struggling to meet a goal for forming a common currency union so they can compete globally with the United States, appear unlikely to meet a much higher target of 3 percent deficit-to-gross domestic product in 1997.
Reaser said a meaningful cut in capital gains taxes, favoured by Congress, would have a great impact in stimulating the economy in the longer term.

"The great value of it is long-term though it also would produce some near-term gains in revenues by encouraging selling of stocks," Reaser said. "But long-term it increases the after-tax return on investment and savings and that's more valuable in creating capital."

Sinai said research indicates that reduced taxation on capital gains like those made from selling stocks and bonds "can unleash a flood of money early, the so-called 'unlocking' effect as investors take gains."

Sinai said he would go further than so far has been proposed and have no taxation of capital gains, noting that puts him in company with a position that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has advocated separately.
